title: Vomiting infant: intussusception
stem: Paediatric area. Jason, 9 months, has had episodes of screaming and drawing his legs up since this morning, with vomiting, and he is pale and floppy between episodes. His mother noticed a 'jelly-like' red nappy an hour ago. HR 170, CRT 3 s, temperature 37.6 °C. Take a history and plan.
notes:
Checked against RCH Melbourne and RCS/BAPS guidance on intussusception, and NICE NG143 traffic-light system.

Intussusception (6 months to 2 years): episodic inconsolable crying with drawing up of legs, pallor and lethargy between episodes, vomiting (becoming bilious), late 'redcurrant jelly' stool, a sausage-shaped mass in the right upper quadrant. Bilious vomiting in any infant is a surgical emergency (malrotation with volvulus until proven otherwise). Ultrasound (target/doughnut sign) is the investigation of choice. Resuscitate with 10–20 mL/kg boluses (10 mL/kg per RCUK), IV access, bloods, NG tube, analgesia, and contact the paediatric surgeon; air enema reduction by radiology with the surgical team present if stable and no peritonitis or perforation; surgery if these fail or the child is peritonitic/shocked.

Other causes of vomiting in infants to consider in the history: gastroenteritis, UTI, pyloric stenosis (2–8 weeks, projectile, non-bilious, hypochloraemic alkalosis), DKA, raised ICP, NAI, sepsis. Your notes list 'paediatric vomiting' as a topic without detail.
